*this dictionary lists basic words. Lojban is a live and dynamic language and accumulates more words over time.
{{vajni|The general rule is that <u>everyone is free to create new words</u> in Lojban. When you need a new word consult Lojbanists to discuss a place structure and the sounding of it.}}
*examples are provided only for most useful places of verbs. Places not listed here may be sometimes used by people in real conversations. Feel free to consult them on the meaning of those places.
**some examples represent advanced style. I added them to show different (sometimes more powerful) applications of a word. You may try to analyze them later.
*for verbs with many places you may remember only a few of them. Not all places are always needed. Practice will allow you to gradually internalize needed places while speaking to Lojbanists in real time.
==Types of places==
Each place in Lojban can contain one of the following:
*clause (or it's particular cases: property,
*entity or text
*number
Those are put in brackets after each place, for example:
:'''catlu''' — ''x<sub>1</sub><sub>(entity)</sub>''  looks at  ''x<sub>2</sub><sub>(clause)</sub>''
{{notci|In case of doubt with places open this dictionary and look at the examples for the word you need. At least one of the usage examples will have all places filled.}}
===Entity and clause===
''Entity'' place in a noun matches an ''entity'' place of the main verb:
{{mu|lo plise cu grute|Apple is a fruit.}}
{{gl|plise|x<sub>1</sub> (entity) is an apple of species x<sub>2</sub>}}
{{gl|grute|x<sub>1</sub> (entity) is a fruit of plant x<sub>2</sub>}}
::- here the first place of '''plise''' is an entity and it matches the first place of '''grute''' which is also an entity.

''Clause'' place in a noun matches a ''clause'' place of the main verb.
:It means that the place is filled either with a clause or with another place of ''clause'' type:
{{mu|lo crisa cu citsi}}
{{gl|crisa|x<sub>1</sub> (clause) is a summer}}
{{gl|citsi|x<sub>1</sub> (clause) is a season}}
::- here the first place of '''crisa''' is a clause and it matches the first place of '''citsi''' which is also a clause.

{{mu|mi djica lo se nitcu|I want what is needed.}}
{{gl|djica|x<sub>1</sub> wants x<sub>2</sub> (clause)}}
{{gl|nitcu|x<sub>1</sub> needs x<sub>2</sub> (clause)}}
{{gl|se nitcu|x<sub>1</sub> (clause) is needed by x<sub>2</sub>}}
::- here the second place of '''djica''' is a clause and it matches the second place of '''nitcu''' which is also a clause.
{{mu|lo nicte cu nu lo solri na te gusni|Nighttime is when the Sun isn't shining.}}
{{gl|nicte|x<sub>1</sub> (clause) is a nighttime}}
::- here we have a clause created using '''nu''' and it matches the first place of '''nicte''' which is also a clause.
===Property (infinitive)===
''Property'' is a special kind of clause. It contains a '''ce'u''' particle:
{{mupli|'''mi gleki lo ka ce'u prami''' means the same as<br>'''mi gleki lo nu mi prami'''<br>''I am happy that I love'', ''I am happy of loving (someone).}}
{{mupli|'''mi gleki lo ka prami ce'u''' means the same as<br>'''mi gleki lo nu prami mi'''<br>''I am happy that someone loves me'', ''I am happy of being loved (by someone)}}
The particle '''ce'u''' is used for referring to the noun from the outside verb.
*Definitions of verbs usually explicitly specify to what place '''ce'u''' refers to:
{{mu|pu betri mi|It was a tragedy to me.}}
{{gl|betri|x<sub>1</sub><sub>(property of x2)</sub>  is a tragedy for  x<sub>2</sub><sub>(entity)</sub>}}
*If not explained in the dictionary then '''ce'u''' in the first place of the verb refers to the 2nd place of the verb like in the previous example.

*If not explained in the dictionary then '''ce'u''' in another place refers to the 1st place of the verb:
{{mu|mi kakne lo ka limna|I am able to swim.}}
{{gl|kakne|x<sub>1</sub><sub>(entity)</sub> is capable of doing x<sub>2</sub><sub>(property of x1)</sub>}}

There is also a rule that the first omitted noun in the embedded clause is automatically assigned the value of '''ce'u''' if '''ka''' is used in the beginning of the embedded clause. So we can make the first sentence shorter:
{{mupli|'''mi gleki lo ka prami''' means the same as<br>'''mi gleki lo ke ce'u prami'''<br>''I am happy that I love'', ''I am happy of loving (someone).}}
However, compare:
{{mupli|'''mi gleki lo ka prami ce'u'''}}
Here, in order to omit '''ce'u''' we need to somehow fill the first noun so that '''ce'u''' goes to the next unfilled noun. Here is how we cand do that:
{{mupli|'''mi gleki lo ka do prami''' means the same as<br>'''mi gleki lo ka do prami ce'u''' or '''mi gleki lo nu do prami mi'''<br>''I am happy that you love me'', ''I am happy of being loved by you''.}}

Some properties can refer equally to several places. For example, for '''zmadu''' and '''mleca''' the particle '''ce'u''' refers equally to the first two places:
{{mu|mi zmadu do lo ka clani vau lo centre be li mu|I am 5 centimeters taller than you.|I am more than you in length by 5 centimeters.}}
{{gl|zmadu|x<sub>1</sub> (any type) exceeds or is more than x<sub>2</sub> (any type) in x<sub>3</sub> (property of x<sub>1</sub> and x<sub>2</sub> with {kau}) by amount x<sub>4</sub>}}
::- here, '''mi''' and '''do''' are compared, and '''ce'u''' in the third place refers to '''mi''' and '''do''' equally.

A very special case is '''simxu''' that has in its second place two '''ce'u''':
{{mu|mi ce do simxu lo ka ce'u ce'u prami|You and I love each other.}}
The first place of '''simxu''' is one or several nouns connected with '''ce'''.

The second place of '''simxu''' is an abstraction. The first <u>two</u> unfilled places take have '''ce'u''' implied. So you can remove both '''ce'u''' in this example:
{{mu|mi ce do simxu lo ka prami|You and I love each other.}}
'''ka''' and '''ce'u''' are also used to express infinitives:
{{mu|mi djica lo ka pinxe''' or '''mi djica lo nu mi pinxe|I want to drink.}}

===Other types===
''Proposition'' is a place filled with '''du'u'''. It works exactly as '''nu''' but is traditionally used with some places and always mentioned for them in the dictionary:
{{gl|djuno|x<sub>1</sub> (entity) knows that x<sub>2</sub> (proposition) is true}}
{{mu|mi djuno lo du'u do stati|I know that you are smart.}}

Instead of ''property'' you may use another type of clause with '''nu''' or '''du'u'''. Compare
{{mu|mi djica lo ka sipna|I want to sleep.}}
{{mu|mi djica lo nu do sipna|I want you to sleep.|I want that you sleep.}}

''Text'' place is filled with quotes and start with '''zo''', '''lu ... li'u''', '''zoi''', '''zo'oi''' or some other particles. The dictionary provides examples of such places.

Numbers are marked with '''li''':
{{mu|ti mitre li mu|This is 5 meters long.}}
:or a &quot;number&quot; place from another verb: '''lo namcu''', '''lo se mitre'''.

There are other more rare types of places like ''taxon''. ''taxon'' is filled with names of species, plant varieties, which start with '''la'''.

==='''tu'a''' and '''zo'ei'''===

{{mu|ra na nitcu lo ka co'e|He does not have to do this.}}
:'''co'e''' — elliptical/unspecified verb. Often translated with ''this'', ''that'', ''it''.
{{mu|ma pu co'e|Who did it?}}
{{mu|mi curmi lo nu do co'e|I will give you permission to do it.}}
So '''co'e''' is a verb that is known from context. '''mi co'e''' might mean ''I am doing you know what'', or ''You know who I am.''

While '''zo'e''' is the ‘don't care’ noun, '''co'e''' is the ‘don't care’ verb. For example, when I say '''mi klama lo barja''', I'm not bothering to specify my point of origin, route, or vehicle. And when I say '''mi co'e lo barja''' I don't specify what I'm doing to the bar, probably I'm visiting it. So '''mi co'e lo barja''' means something like ''I thingummy the bar'': the bar and I are in some relationship, but I'm not bothering to say what it is. I might be going to it, coming from it, sleeping in it, refurbishing it, or hearing about my neighbor getting drunk in it once. It just doesn't matter enough for me to say what.

The verb '''djica''' requires us to specify an event that one desires.
:'''mi djica lo nu mi citka lo plise'''
:''I want to eat an apple.''
Okay, but usually we just say in English ''I want an apple''. We can't desire the apple itself, we want to <u>do</u> something with it.

Here we can omit the second '''mi''' and replace the verb ''to eat'' with '''co'e'''.
:'''mi djica lo nu co'e lo plise'''
:''I want something to do with an apple.''
So I let it be up to context what abstraction about the apple I desire.

There is a compact abbreviation for '''lo nu co'e''' which is '''tu'a''':
:'''mi djica tu'a lo plise'''
:''I want an apple.''

'''tu'a''' takes a noun and converts it to an elliptical abstraction which has something to do with that noun. One always has to guess what abstraction the speaker means by '''tu'a''' + the noun, so it should only be used when context makes it easy to guess.

Another example:
{{gl|gasnu|x1 does/brings about x2 (volition not implied)}}
:'''za'a do gasnu tu'a lo skami'''
:''I see that you make the computer do something.''

There are situations where you cannot use '''tu'a''', even though it would seem suitable. These situations are when I don't want the resulting noun to be an abstraction, but a concrete noun. In this case, one can use '''zo'e pe''' or its abbreviation '''zo'ei'''.
{{mu|mi djuno zo'ei do''' or '''mi djuno zo'e pe do|I know about you, I know something about you}}
===Advanced situations===
These last two rules can be found in colloquial speech. They are usually avoided by careful speakers. However, if you bump into them you will know how to deal with them.
----
Putting an ''entity'' place into a ''clause'' place denotes an obvious relation:
{{mu|mi djica lo plise|I want an apple.}}
:The second place of '''djica''' is a clause. Thus '''lo plise''', ''an apple'' plays some role in that clause. Probably it means:
{{mu|mi djica lo nu mi citka lo plise|I want to eat an apple.}}
:but maybe I just want to hold an apple in my hand. If you need vagueness or just lazy to say more you can use this method.

{{mu|do nabmi|You are a problem.}}
{{gl|nabmi|x<sub>1</sub><sub>(clause)</sub> is a problem...}}
::probably means that there is something problematic with you.

:This situation is also called &quot;grammatical raising&quot; in English.
----
A ''clause'' place in a noun can be put into an ''entity'' place of the main verb:
{{mu|mi klama lo nu penmi|I go to a meeting.}}
{{gl|klama|x<sub>1</sub><sub>(entity)</sub> goes to x<sub>2</sub><sub>(entity)</sub>...}}
:The second place of '''klama''' denotes a place where you go. '''lo nu penmi''' denotes a process of meeting, thus we assume that here it is bound to some location where I go.

:Another example:
{{mu|lo ka kucli pu catra lo mlatu|Curiosity killed the cat.}}
:: - here ''curiosity'' is turned into an entity that is able to kill. As it's a clause with '''ka''' it has to refer to some place. :As the definition of '''catra''' says nothing about such situation we assume that it refers to the first unfilled place: here it's x<sub>2</sub>. Thus, it's the curiosity of the cat that killed it.
